findings.title: SQL query built with string interpolation

evidence.description: A SQL statement is built by string formatting/concatenation instead of bound parameters.
evidence.sanitized_code: cur.execute(f"SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'")

findings.impact: If attacker-controlled data reaches the query, an attacker may read, modify or delete data, bypass authentication or, depending on the DBMS, execute commands.
findings.exploitability: Exploitable when any interpolated value is attacker-influenced and not strictly validated (e.g. integer cast or allow-list).
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: Use parameterized queries / prepared statements or the ORM query builder. Never interpolate values into SQL; allow-list identifiers (column/table names) if they must be dynamic.
remediation.security_test: Call the code path with a controlled payload such as `' OR '1'='1` against a local test database and assert that no extra rows are returned and no SQL error leaks.
remediation.regression_test: Unit test that asserts the query is executed with placeholders and a separate parameters tuple (mock the cursor) and that legitimate lookups still return the expected row.
remediation.verification: Run the regression test and the existing test suite; confirm the payload is treated as a literal value.

findings.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference on invoice retrieval

evidence.description: The handler loads an invoice by the path parameter invoice_id and returns it without checking that the invoice belongs to the authenticated user. No authorization decorator or ownership filter exists on this route or in a before_request hook (reviewed app/app.py in full).
evidence.sanitized_code:
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ?", (invoice_id,))
return jsonify(cur.fetchone())

findings.impact: Any user who can reach the endpoint can enumerate invoice ids and read other customers' invoices (personal and financial data).
findings.exploitability: Trivial when invoice ids are sequential; requires only network access to the endpoint.
findings.business_impact: Exposure of customer financial data; likely reportable privacy incident.

remediation.recommendation: Scope the query to the current user (WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?) and return 404 when the invoice is not owned by the caller. Centralize the check in a reusable authorization helper.
remediation.fixed_code_example:
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?", (invoice_id, current_user.id))
row = cur.fetchone()
if row is None:
    abort(404)
remediation.security_test: With two local test users A and B, request B's invoice id as A and assert 404 and no invoice data in the body.
remediation.regression_test: Assert that A can still read A's own invoice (200, same payload as before).
remediation.verification: Run both tests; review the other object-returning routes for the same pattern.

notes: confirmed by code reading; no dynamic test executed

findings.title: OS command execution through a shell

evidence.description: An OS command is executed through a shell or with a dynamically built command string.

findings.impact: Attacker-controlled data in the command can lead to arbitrary command execution with the application's privileges.
findings.exploitability: Exploitable when any part of the command string is attacker-influenced.
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: Avoid the shell: pass an argument list (shell=False / execFile / ProcessBuilder with separate args), validate input against an allow-list and prefer native libraries over shelling out.
remediation.fixed_code_example: subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], check=True, timeout=5)  # host validated against an allow-list/regex
remediation.security_test: In a sandbox, pass `127.0.0.1; id` and assert the command fails validation and `id` is never executed (mock subprocess).
remediation.regression_test: Assert subprocess is called with a list and shell=False, and that valid hosts still work.
remediation.verification: Run the tests; grep for remaining shell=True / exec( usages in the module.

findings.title: JWT decoded without signature verification

evidence.description: JWT validation is weakened (signature, algorithm or claim checks disabled).

findings.impact: Attackers may forge or replay tokens, impersonating users or escalating privileges.
findings.exploitability: Exploitable when the token is used for authentication/authorization decisions.
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: Always verify the signature with an explicit algorithm allow-list, and validate exp, nbf, iss and aud.
remediation.security_test: Present a token signed with a different key and an `alg: none` token; assert both are rejected (401).
remediation.regression_test: Assert valid tokens are still accepted and expired tokens are rejected.
remediation.verification: Run tests covering signature, expiry, issuer and audience.

findings.title: Weak password hashing (fast, unsalted hash)

evidence.description: A weak hash algorithm (MD5/SHA-1) is used.

findings.impact: If used for passwords, signatures or integrity, collisions or fast brute force undermine the control.
findings.exploitability: Only a vulnerability when the hash protects a security property; checksums/cache keys are usually acceptable.
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: For passwords use Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt with per-user salt; for integrity use SHA-256+ or HMAC.
remediation.fixed_code_example:
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
hash = PasswordHasher().hash(password)
remediation.security_test: Assert stored password hashes use the new algorithm prefix (e.g. $argon2id$).
remediation.regression_test: Assert login still works, including a migration path for legacy hashes.
remediation.verification: Run tests; confirm the purpose of each MD5/SHA-1 usage.

findings.title: Dangerous Linux capabilities added

evidence.description: The container/workload runs with elevated privileges or host access.

findings.impact: A compromise of the container can escalate to the host or cluster.
findings.exploitability: Relevant if the workload is deployed with this configuration.
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: Run as a non-root user, drop all capabilities, forbid privilege escalation, avoid host namespaces and the Docker socket, and enable a read-only root filesystem.
remediation.fixed_code_example:
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
remediation.security_test: Use a policy check (e.g. Kubernetes Pod Security 'restricted' admission, or `docker inspect`) to assert the settings.
remediation.regression_test: Assert the service still starts and passes health checks as non-root.
remediation.verification: Deploy to a test cluster/namespace with restricted policy.

findings.title: Exception details returned to the client

evidence.description: Exception details or stack traces are returned to the client.

findings.impact: Internal paths, queries, versions or secrets may be disclosed and aid further attacks.
findings.exploitability: Relevant for responses reachable by untrusted users.
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: Return generic error messages with a correlation id and log details server-side.
remediation.security_test: Trigger the error path and assert the body contains no stack trace.
remediation.regression_test: Assert error responses keep the expected status code.
remediation.verification: Run tests.

findings.title: Ingress open to 0.0.0.0/0

evidence.description: A resource is exposed to the internet or allows unrestricted network access.

findings.impact: Services become reachable by any attacker on the internet.
findings.exploitability: Relevant if the exposed port/service is not intended to be public.
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: Restrict CIDR ranges to known networks, place services behind load balancers/WAF and use private subnets.
remediation.security_test: Run a policy check (e.g. checkov, tfsec/trivy config) in CI.
remediation.regression_test: Verify legitimate clients still connect from allowed ranges.
remediation.verification: Run `terraform plan` and review the security group diff.

findings.title: Base image not pinned (latest or no tag)

evidence.description: The base image is not pinned to a specific version/digest.

findings.impact: Builds are not reproducible and may silently pull compromised or breaking images.
findings.exploitability: Supply-chain risk; exploitation requires a compromised or changed upstream image.
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: Pin images to a version tag and preferably a digest (image@sha256:...), and update via automated PRs.
remediation.security_test: Policy check in CI that rejects untagged/latest images.
remediation.regression_test: Rebuild and run the image test suite.
remediation.verification: Rebuild the image.

findings.title: Directory listing enabled

evidence.description: Web server configuration discloses information (directory listing, version banners).

findings.impact: Helps attackers enumerate files and fingerprint versions.
findings.exploitability: Relevant for internet-facing servers.
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: Disable directory listing and version banners.
remediation.security_test: Request a directory without index locally and assert 403/404.
remediation.regression_test: Verify normal pages are still served.
remediation.verification: Reload and test.

findings.title: Workflow without explicit permissions block

evidence.description: CI/CD workflow configuration allows untrusted input or excessive privileges.

findings.impact: Attackers may execute code in CI, steal secrets or push malicious artifacts.
findings.exploitability: Exploitable via pull requests, issues or comments from untrusted users, depending on triggers.
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: Use least-privilege `permissions:`, never interpolate untrusted event fields into `run:` (use env vars), avoid checking out PR code in pull_request_target, and pin actions to full commit SHAs.
remediation.security_test: Review with actionlint/zizmor or equivalent workflow linters.
remediation.regression_test: Run the workflow on a test PR.
remediation.verification: Check the workflow run logs and permissions summary.

findings.title: Dockerfile has no USER instruction (defaults to root)

evidence.description: The container/workload runs with elevated privileges or host access.

findings.impact: A compromise of the container can escalate to the host or cluster.
findings.exploitability: Relevant if the workload is deployed with this configuration.
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: Run as a non-root user, drop all capabilities, forbid privilege escalation, avoid host namespaces and the Docker socket, and enable a read-only root filesystem.
remediation.fixed_code_example:
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
remediation.security_test: Use a policy check (e.g. Kubernetes Pod Security 'restricted' admission, or `docker inspect`) to assert the settings.
remediation.regression_test: Assert the service still starts and passes health checks as non-root.
remediation.verification: Deploy to a test cluster/namespace with restricted policy.

findings.title: Weak hash algorithm (MD5/SHA-1)

evidence.description: A weak hash algorithm (MD5/SHA-1) is used.

findings.impact: If used for passwords, signatures or integrity, collisions or fast brute force undermine the control.
findings.exploitability: Only a vulnerability when the hash protects a security property; checksums/cache keys are usually acceptable.
findings.business_impact: Not assessed by the scanner; evaluate against the affected asset and data classification.

remediation.recommendation: For passwords use Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt with per-user salt; for integrity use SHA-256+ or HMAC.
remediation.fixed_code_example:
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
hash = PasswordHasher().hash(password)
remediation.security_test: Assert stored password hashes use the new algorithm prefix (e.g. $argon2id$).
remediation.regression_test: Assert login still works, including a migration path for legacy hashes.
remediation.verification: Run tests; confirm the purpose of each MD5/SHA-1 usage.

triage.justification: MD5 is used only to build a non-secret cache key (cache_key); no security property depends on collision resistance.
